analysis: The closest option now implements all four PPLE disciplines with sustained political, economic, legal and behavioural study. Replaced the oversized mathematics bundle with political philosophy, constitutional law and actual public policy; organisational psychology replaces lifespan development, and human-rights law/philosophy replaces empire history for more direct PPLE substance.

The behavioural option retains psychological/economic explanation and adds actual public-policy analysis in place of accounting. Data science, machine learning, negotiation and ethics differentiate its empirical policy focus. The legal option retains a sustained law sequence and its distinct normative/qualitative/civil-society focus; its valid selections required rescheduling, not replacement.

Every course contribution was reconsidered from its available profile or description. Description-only behavioural economics, econometrics, public policy and social-movement study receive full consideration for what their descriptions support. Sixteen important, identifiable partial relationships replace the blanket credit-bucket no-match. Law/Behaviour, specialist seminars, philosophy of science, cultural psychology, Research Lab, thesis and open choice retain reasoned blanks. No identical-credit or disciplinary-equivalence requirement is imposed.

All five original offering conflicts are repaired by moving introductory economics, criminal law and behavioural economics to currently planned terms. Three schedules pass all formal rules and the six-term horizon. Advisory sequencing puts brain/behaviour, social psychology and statistics before experimental methods, comparative politics before EU/policy work and data foundations before machine learning. Each pair passes thirty EC and substantive distinctness. Optional research appears with the actual thesis outside scheduled credits.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, literature evaluation, civic collaboration and reflective practice provide the first-year common foundation.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.contribution: introduces economic reasoning about markets, resources and government as a foundation for political-economic analysis

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.contribution: examines open-economy macroeconomic dynamics, goods, financial and labour markets, inflation, growth, and fiscal and monetary policy using formal models

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.contribution: examines microeconomic decisions, incentives and behavioural responses, supporting analysis of policy effects and political-economic choices

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.contribution: examines public intervention, equity, public goods, taxation, education, health and social insurance through policy models and research

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.contribution: develops econometric estimation, statistical tests and an empirical paper for analysing causal and predictive economic relationships relevant to policy

BENECON314.name: Behavioral Economics
BENECON314.contribution: examines how biases, heuristics and framing change decisions through the integration of psychology and economics, including experiments

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.contribution: develops empirical design, measurement, sampling, statistics and a complete student data-collection project as research foundations for political inquiry

BENLEAD311.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
BENLEAD311.contribution: examines individual motivation, teams, leadership, power and organisational change, and develops research plans and a systematic literature review for organisational cases

BENLEAD312.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
BENLEAD312.contribution: develops bargaining, strategic choice, trust, framing and conflict management through negotiation simulations and an applied scenario project

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.contribution: develops data cleaning, transformation, visualisation and applied research in R, supporting empirical investigation of political evidence

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.contribution: develops statistical prediction, regression, classification, model evaluation and data analysis as computational complements to political research

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: introduces legal traditions, social justice and legal reasoning as foundations for studying political institutions and public power

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: examines human-rights law and philosophical claims, dignity, international protection and legal-political arguments

GOSLAWJ211.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
GOSLAWJ211.contribution: examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation and justice through legal cases and a criminology or organised-crime research proposal; it adds a legal perspective on security rather than replacing international-relations theory

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.contribution: examines international legal sources, states and institutions, force, conflict, human rights, economic and environmental law, and the political dimensions of law

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: compares constitutions, legislatures, executives, courts, judicial review, rights and administrative remedies as structures of public power

GOSLAWJ311.name: Principles of Private Law
GOSLAWJ311.contribution: examines property, tort and contract rights and obligations across legal systems through case analysis, comparative research and simulated mediation

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.contribution: examines EU institutions, competences, supremacy, citizenship, free movement and judicial remedies through legal cases

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: develops moral reasoning and independent ethical arguments relevant to public responsibilities and competing political values

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: examines historical and contemporary political thought, authority, rights and society through original texts and normative argument

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: examines democracy, autocratisation, institutions, participation and political behaviour through empirical comparison and a research memo

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.contribution: examines competing international-relations theories, geopolitics, conflicts and global cooperation through case research and a UN simulation

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: examines EU institutions, integration, representation, legitimacy and policymaking, with an empirical research project on parliamentary amendments and interest influence

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.contribution: examines policy-making phases, policy actors and alternative analytical frameworks through a sugar-policy case and policy memos

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: examines conflict, inequality, identity and colonial legacies through interdisciplinary approaches to security, peacebuilding and justice, including a policy brief

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: develops qualitative interviewing, documentary inquiry, interpretation and reflexivity for social and political research

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.contribution: examines social movements, environmental justice and collective action through feminist, anticolonial and other perspectives

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: examines civil society, trust, solidarity, hegemony and social repair through theory and research on an organisation or initiative

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.contribution: introduces psychological and neural explanations of learning, personality, social influence and behaviour, supporting the psychological strand without substituting for social or political theory

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: examines social influence, group processes, prejudice, aggression and prosocial behaviour as psychological foundations for political interaction

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.contribution: develops experimental design and statistical analysis of multivariable models, categorical outcomes and latent constructs, with data-analysis papers and a research poster

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.contribution: examines youth radicalisation, risk, belonging, inclusive education and prevention through research-based teacher resources and a youth toolkit

alignment.rationale: Both introduce economic choice, strategic interaction, firms, markets and the allocation of resources. UvA gives additional emphasis to institutional change, inequality and sustainability.
Both examine macroeconomic output, employment, inflation, growth, money and the IS-LM framework. UCR extends these foundations into open-economy analysis and policy.

Both develop regression-based empirical analysis and research reporting. UvA combines quantitative political analysis with qualitative methods; UCR concentrates on economic estimation, statistical tests and an empirical paper.
Both develop research questions, design, measurement, ethics and empirical inquiry through a student research project. UCR also provides introductory statistical analysis.
Both critically examine human-rights law, philosophical justifications, universality and rights in political and social contexts. UvA combines these perspectives in an integrative seminar.

Both examine the formal organisation of public power, state institutions and legal constraints on authority. UCR concentrates on constitutional and administrative law; UvA also analyses broader political power and decision-making processes.

Both examine competing normative theories, including consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, and apply moral arguments to social questions. UvA integrates these with legal philosophy and theories of justice.
Both examine political authority, rights, legitimacy and justice through classic and contemporary political thought and normative argument.
Both compare democracy, democratisation, authoritarian change, institutions and explanations of regime trajectories.
Both introduce international-relations theories and apply them to global power, conflict and cooperation involving states and other actors.
Both examine European integration, EU institutions, decision-making and legitimacy in relation to contemporary political challenges. UCR adds an empirical parliamentary project.
Both examine public policy, governance actors and alternative frameworks for understanding collective responses to social problems. UCR applies these through a policy case and memos.
Both examine causes and dynamics of conflict, international security and approaches to peace, including legal, political and social perspectives.

Both examine solidarity and the relationship between individual action and collective social life. UCR centres civil society, trust and social theory; UvA integrates psychological and economic explanations of cooperation.
Both examine social perception, attitudes, influence, prejudice, group processes and aggression through psychological research.

Both develop applied statistical analysis of group differences, relationships and multivariable models using real data and statistical software. UCR situates the methods in health and behavioural research.
Academic writing and argument occur across the UCR options, but no selected course provides the dedicated rhetorical analysis and public-speaking practice of this course.
The selected philosophy and methods courses support reasoning and research, but no dedicated philosophy-of-social-science course is selected.
The UCR legal, behavioural and negotiation courses provide complementary perspectives, but none centres the empirical mechanisms of legal compliance across the scope of Law and Behaviour.
The UCR courses address conflict and radicalisation, but no additional course is counted as the dedicated interdisciplinary security-research seminar.
Applied UCR projects support social engagement, but no additional course reproduces this reflective integrative seminar and its student interventions.
The UCR economics and institutional courses support political-economic inquiry, but none supplies this dedicated historical and international state–market relations sequence.
Political institutions and social psychology contribute to this theme elsewhere; no additional course centres the seminar’s specific democracy, truth, media and political-epistemology focus.
Social and organisational psychology are represented elsewhere. No selected course centres the cultural and cross-cultural psychology of this course.
UCR methods courses develop research designs and projects, but they are not counted again as the distinct interdisciplinary Research Lab.

Comparative politics and social psychology have stronger primary placements elsewhere. No additional selected course provides this dedicated survey of citizens’ and elites’ political attitudes and behaviour.
No compulsory individual interdisciplinary thesis is scheduled at UCR. Optional independent research appears separately outside the scheduled credits.
Open elective space remains unspecified; no particular elective or internship is invented.
